findings.name: Introspection exposed
findings.evidence: Introspection returned the full schema (12 types) with NO token — anyone on the internet can read it.
findings.fix: Disable introspection in production (and block __schema and __type for anonymous users).

findings.name: No depth limit
findings.evidence: The API answered a depth-50 query (cost ~2601) and never refused — no depth limit was found up to depth 50.
findings.fix: Enforce a query-depth limit (5–10 is typical) before the query reaches the engine.

findings.name: Batching enabled
findings.evidence: Array batching works: one request with 100 queries returned 100 responses — a rate-limit bypass and a DoS amplifier.
findings.fix: Disable array batching, or cap the batch size (10 is a common limit) and count batched operations against the rate limit.

findings.name: Alias overloading
findings.evidence: Alias overloading works: one query with 101 aliases returned data for the last alias (a100) — the engine resolved 101 copies of the same field.
findings.fix: Limit the number of aliases per query (and dedupe identical fields before execution).

findings.name: Field duplication
findings.evidence: Field duplication accepted: the same field 50 times in one selection set was executed without complaint.
findings.fix: Deduplicate identical fields before execution, and count duplicates towards the complexity limit.

findings.name: Directive overloading
findings.evidence: Directive overloading accepted: one field with 10 unknown directives executed without complaint.
findings.fix: Limit the number of directives per query, and reject unknown directives instead of ignoring them.

findings.name: Field returns data without auth
findings.evidence: Field 'me' returns data with NO token: object[3 keys]
findings.fix: Enforce authorization on 'me' — check the token before the resolver runs, not after.

findings.name: Field returns data without auth
findings.evidence: Field 'admin' returns data with NO token: string[21 chars]
findings.fix: Enforce authorization on 'admin' — check the token before the resolver runs, not after.

findings.name: Field returns data without auth
findings.evidence: Field 'user' returns data with NO token: object[3 keys]
findings.fix: Enforce authorization on 'user' — check the token before the resolver runs, not after.

findings.name: Field returns data without auth
findings.evidence: Field 'users' returns data with NO token: list[3 items]
findings.fix: Enforce authorization on 'users' — check the token before the resolver runs, not after.

findings.name: IDOR — another user's object
findings.evidence: IDOR: the scan token (user 1) fetched ANOTHER user's object: user 2; user 3
findings.fix: Scope object access to the owner (or an admin) — check the token's user id against the requested id in the resolver.

findings.name: Mutation without auth
findings.fix: Require authentication for every mutation — mutations change state, queries only read it.

findings.name: Mutation without auth
findings.fix: Require authentication for every mutation — mutations change state, queries only read it.

findings.name: GET-based queries (CSRF angle)
findings.evidence: GET-based queries work: the same query runs over GET (curl 'http://127.0.0.1:33641/graphql?query={%20__typename%20}'). If this API ever uses cookie auth, that is a CSRF vector.
findings.fix: Accept GraphQL only over POST with a JSON body, or require a CSRF token / custom header on GET.

findings.name: Sensitive field exposed
findings.evidence: Sensitive field exposed: passwordHash returned without a token: string[38 chars]
findings.fix: Never expose password hashes (or secrets/tokens) through the API — remove the field from the schema, or gate it behind an admin-only resolver.

findings.name: Subscriptions supported
findings.evidence: Subscriptions supported: HTTP subscription returns event data — a live event stream is an unauthenticated push channel and a denial-of-service shape (one client, many open streams).
findings.fix: Disable subscriptions unless the API needs them; require authentication before the subscription is accepted, and cap concurrent subscriptions per client.

findings.name: Persisted queries accepted (APQ)
findings.evidence: Persisted queries accepted (APQ): the hash-only request was answered PersistedQueryNotFound (the server looked the hash up) and the hash+query request registered and executed — clients can run queries by hash alone, which bypasses any inspection that reads the query text.
findings.fix: Disable APQ unless clients need it; if it is needed, allow only hashes registered at deploy time, and apply the same depth / complexity / auth checks to persisted queries as to plain ones.

findings.name: File upload accepted
findings.evidence: File upload accepted: the multipart upload executed and returned object[2 keys] — an upload endpoint is a classic attack surface (stored content, parsing, size).
findings.fix: Disable file uploads unless the API needs them; validate the file type and size server-side, store uploads outside the web root, and require authentication for the upload mutation.

findings.name: No rate limiting observed
findings.evidence: No rate limiting observed: 20 identical queries in a row all answered (no 429, no slowdown). Absence of evidence is not proof — but nothing throttled the flood.
findings.fix: Add per-client rate limiting (and count batched operations against it).
